flawed_step: The claim that the bridgeless hypothesis can be dropped. A cubic graph with bridges can have no perfect matching.
counterexample: A 16-vertex connected cubic graph. Start with a center vertex c. For i=1,2,3, build a gadget G_i with vertices a_i, p_i, q_i, r_i, s_i and edges p_i r_i, p_i s_i, q_i r_i, q_i s_i, r_i s_i, a_i p_i, a_i q_i. This is K4 on {p,q,r,s} with edge pq removed, plus a new vertex a joined to p and q. Then add the edges c a_1, c a_2, c a_3. Degree check: c has a1,a2,a3; a_i has c,p_i,q_i; p_i has r_i,s_i,a_i; q_i has r_i,s_i,a_i; r_i has p_i,q_i,s_i; s_i has p_i,q_i,r_i. Every vertex has degree 3, there are 24 edges, the graph is simple, and it is connected through c. Removing c leaves three components with 5 vertices each, so each is odd. In a perfect matching, every odd component must have some vertex matched to a vertex outside it. The only outside neighbor is c, and c can be matched only once. Three components need it, so no perfect matching exists (Tutte's condition fails: o(G-c)=3>1=|{c}|).
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The standard 16-vertex cubic graph with three bridges meeting at one central vertex has no perfect matching: removing that vertex leaves three odd components, which breaks Tutte's condition.
